question.problem:
In a biased coin, $60%$ of the flips land on heads. Using the normal approximation to the binomial distribution, estimate the probability that the coin lands on heads at least $21$ times out of $50$ flips. Give your final answer to $3$ decimal places.

*Hint: The data below is taken from the table of values of the cumulative distribution function $Φ(z)$ for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.03\,$ | $\,0.04\,$ | $\,0.05\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,-2.9\,$ | $\,0.0017\,$ | $\,0.0016\,$ | $\,0.0016\,$ |
| $\,-2.8\,$ | $\,0.0023\,$ | $\,0.0023\,$ | $\,0.0022\,$ |
| $\,-2.7\,$ | $\,0.0032\,$ | $\,0.0031\,$ | $\,0.0030\,$ |
question.worked_solution:
Given a binomial random variable $X∼B(n,p),$ if 

- $np>5,$ and

- $n(1-p)>5,$

we can approximate $X$ as a normal random variable $Y$ with mean $\mu =np$ and variance ${\sigma }^{2}=np(1-p),$ that is, 

$$
Y∼N(np,np(1-p)).
$$

Here, we have $n=50$ and $p=0.6.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}np & =50\cdot 0.6 \\  & =30 \\  & >5\,✓ \\ n(1-p) & =50\cdot (1-0.6) \\  & =20 \\  & >5.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can approximate our binomial random variable $X$ with a normal random variable $Y$ with mean

$$
\mu =np=(50)(0.6)=30
$$

and variance

$$
{\sigma }^{2}=np(1-p)=(50)(0.6)(1-0.6)=12.
$$

That is, we can approximate $X$ by $Y∼N(30,12).$

Now, we can estimate the desired probability $P(X\ge 21).$ Using a continuity correction, we have

$$
P(X\ge 21)≈P(Y>20.5).
$$

To compute this probability, we transform to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y>20.5) & =1-P(Y\le 20.5) \\  & =1-P(Z\le \frac{20.5-30}{\sqrt{12}}) \\  & ≈1-P(Z\le -2.74) \\  & =1-Φ(-2.74) \\  & =1-0.0031 \\  & =0.9969\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
P(X\ge 21)≈0.997.
$$

Note: Using a software package for the approximation gives a probability of $0.9966.$
